frontend.label: Frontend engineer
frontend.listing: Senior Frontend Engineer — React, TypeScript, design systems. You will own the component library.

hr.question: Tell me about a release that slipped. What did you do about it?

answers.a: Our design-system migration slipped two weeks when a shared modal broke in three products. I cut the release down to the twelve components nobody was blocked on, shipped those on the original date, and told both product leads the same afternoon with a new date for the rest. We hit it, and I added a cross-product smoke test so the next break shows up before release day.
answers.b: It happens sometimes. We talked as a team, worked out what went wrong, and made sure we planned better the next time round.
answers.c: Honestly the whole quarter was difficult. Two people left, the roadmap changed twice, and the design team was rebuilding the tokens underneath us at the same time. Everyone was stretched thin. I think the planning process was the real problem — we commit to dates before the designs are settled, and I have been saying so for a while.

reasons.a: Situation, decision, who you told, and the result — plus a fix that outlived the incident. Ada would push once more on what you gave up by cutting scope, and whether the product leads actually agreed.
reasons.b: Nothing here is yours. Every verb is "we", there is no decision and no result, and the answer would fit any slipped release at any company. Name what you did and what changed because of it.
reasons.c: This is context, not an answer. Ada asked what you did; four sentences in, the subject is still the quarter. The last line also puts the cause outside the room, which is the part an HR interviewer is listening for.

tech.question: A list of a thousand rows re-renders on every keystroke in the filter box. Where do you look first?

answers.a: First, whether the filter state lives above the list — if the input and the rows share a parent, every keystroke re-renders all thousand. I would confirm it on a flamegraph before changing anything, then either move that state down, memoise the row, or debounce the filter. If the rows are genuinely expensive I would virtualise, but that is the last step, not the first.
answers.b: I would add React.memo to the row component and see whether that helps.
answers.c: Re-renders are usually a state colocation problem. React diffs the whole subtree when a parent's state changes, and because that comparison is linear in the number of children you pay for every row. There is nuance here too — the scheduler works in units, so time slicing hides some of the cost, and concurrent rendering changes the picture again.

reasons.a: Measure, then change. You named the likely cause, said how you would confirm it, gave three ordered fixes, and put virtualisation last where it belongs. Turing would follow up on how you choose between moving state and memoising.
reasons.b: A guess, and the one people reach for before they know what is slow. `memo` does nothing when the row props are new objects each render, which is the usual reason this bug survives the first attempt.
reasons.c: Accurate and off target. Turing asked where you would look first and got the reconciler. The depth reads well; nothing in it is a step you would actually take on Monday morning.

product.label: Product manager
product.listing: Product Manager — B2B SaaS, self-serve growth. You will own activation and onboarding.

hr.question: Tell me about a decision you made that turned out to be wrong.

answers.a: I removed our onboarding checklist because activation had not moved in six weeks. Two weeks later, setup tickets were up forty per cent — the checklist was not driving activation, it was preventing confusion, and I had measured the wrong thing. I brought it back behind a flag, wrote down what I had actually been testing, and now I do not remove a surface without a metric for what it was quietly holding up.
answers.b: I have made plenty. You learn from them and move on — I would rather be wrong quickly than right slowly.
answers.c: We decided to build an integrations marketplace. In hindsight the market was not there yet, sales had oversold the demand, and engineering estimated a quarter when it took two. With better data going in, I do not think we would have started.

reasons.a: A real decision, a number that moved the wrong way, and a rule you now follow because of it. Ada would ask who had told you the checklist mattered before you removed it, and what you did with that.
reasons.b: A slogan, not an answer. There is no decision, no consequence and nothing you would do differently — and "wrong quickly" is a value, not an example.
reasons.c: The decision is real; nothing in it is yours. Sales oversold, engineering underestimated, the data was missing. Ada asked what you got wrong — say what you would have decided differently with the information you actually had at the time.

tech.question: Your onboarding rewrite ships and activation drops eight per cent. What do you check first?

answers.a: Whether the number is real. Instrumentation ships with rewrites, so I would confirm the event still fires and that activation is defined the way it was last week. Then split the drop: new users or everyone, all channels or one, all plans or one. Segmentation usually names the cause before any qualitative work does. Session recordings on whichever segment moved, and only then a decision about rolling back.
answers.b: I would roll it back, and then work out what happened.
answers.c: Activation is a lagging indicator, so an eight per cent drop one week in might be noise — you would want the confidence interval before reacting. There is seasonality too, and a rewrite changes the population you are measuring because it changes who gets through the funnel at all, which makes a clean comparison quite hard.

reasons.a: You checked the measurement before the product, then segmented before guessing. Naming rollback as the last decision rather than the first is what separates this from panic. Turing would push on how long you let it run before deciding.
reasons.b: Reasonable instinct, no method. Rolling back destroys the evidence, and you would ship the same rewrite again in six weeks without knowing which part of it hurt.
reasons.c: All true, and none of it is a check. Every sentence is a reason the number might not mean anything. Turing asked what you would do first.

data.label: Data analyst
data.listing: Data Analyst — commercial reporting. SQL, dbt, and a lot of stakeholders.

hr.question: Tell me about a time you had to tell someone their number was wrong.

answers.a: Our head of sales was quoting a conversion rate in board decks that double-counted renewals. I rebuilt it, checked it against the billing export, and took him the two queries side by side before the next board meeting rather than after it. He was annoyed for a day, then asked me to audit the other three metrics in the deck. I now publish the definition next to every number I own.
answers.b: I told them politely and explained the correct figure. They understood, and we moved on.
answers.c: This happens constantly. Most stakeholders pull their own numbers out of the BI tool without checking the definitions, and then two people arrive at a meeting with different figures. I have pushed for a metrics layer for a long time — that is the actual fix, rather than analysts correcting people one at a time.

reasons.a: The person, the error, how you verified it, when you told him, and what changed afterwards. Taking it before the board meeting rather than after is the detail that makes the story yours.
reasons.b: Three sentences with no friction in them. Ada asked about a hard conversation and got a summary of one going well, which is the version people give when they are not describing a real one.
reasons.c: You have answered a different question — what is wrong with the org, not what you did. The proposed fix is sound, and Ada was listening for how you handled a person.

tech.question: A daily revenue dashboard shows a thirty per cent jump overnight. Walk me through your first hour.

answers.a: Whether it is the data or the business. One query on raw rows for yesterday and the day before, no models in the way. If the row count jumped, I would look for a re-run inserting duplicates; if the count is flat and the sum moved, it is real or it is currency. Then the last dbt run and any upstream schema change in that window. Before I tell anyone it is real, I want the same number from a source the pipeline does not touch — usually the billing export.
answers.b: I would ask the engineering team whether anything changed in the pipeline.
answers.c: Thirty per cent is well outside normal variance, so it is almost certainly upstream rather than genuine growth. In my experience these are nearly always duplicate loads — a failed job retries and inserts the same batch twice. I would start from that assumption and work backwards.

reasons.a: Raw rows before models, row count before sum, and a second source before you tell anyone. That last step is the one most answers skip. Turing would ask what you say to the CFO at minute five, before you know.
reasons.b: One question, to someone else, and then you are waiting. Turing asked for your first hour and got your first minute.
reasons.c: A good guess is still a guess. You committed to a cause before running a query, and the answer never checks whether the number is real — if it turns out to be, the hour is spent proving something true is false.

mechanism.title: The questions come from your listing
mechanism.lede: Not a question bank with the job title swapped in. The listing is read for the role, the seniority and the stack, and both rounds are written against what it actually asks for.

listing.title: You paste the listing
listing.body: The one you are actually applying to. It is kept with the interview, so you can practise against the same job again without hunting for it.

rounds.title: Ada opens, Turing follows
rounds.body: An HR round on motivation, conflict and ownership, then a technical round on what the listing names. Two interviewers, two briefs, two voices.

report.title: Every answer is marked as you go
report.body: A score out of five, STAR adherence and a written reason, on every answer. The report at the end collects measurements already taken.

modes.title: Speak it, or type it
modes.lede: The words are the same. Saying them out loud is the part that goes wrong on the day.

voice.title: Voice
voice.body: A real conversation. Ada and Turing speak, you answer out loud, and the next question comes when you stop. There is a microphone check before the room, and captions if you want them.

text.title: Text
text.body: Read the question, write the answer, send it. Same interviewers, same scoring, no microphone — and it works on a train.
text.label: Your answer

report.title: What lands at the end
report.lede: One page to reread the night before, and a PDF that stays yours.

score.def: Out of five, with the HR and technical rounds scored separately — the gap between them is the part you can act on.

rounds.def: What each interviewer made of you, in their own words — including where the two of them disagreed.

strengths.def: Named specifically enough to act on before the real interview. Never "improve your communication".

questions.def: Every question you were asked, the score it got, and the written reason it was marked that way.

transcript.def: Everything asked and everything you said, kept after the interview ends so you can read what you actually answered.

pdf.def: The same report, downloadable, so it survives outside the product.

languages.title: English and Türkçe, both native
languages.lede: Not one written and the other translated. Each interviewer asks in the language of the interview, and the report comes back in it.
languages.enQuestion: This query gets slow at ten million rows. Where do you look first?
languages.trQuestion: Bu sorgu on milyon satırda yavaşlıyor. Önce nereye bakarsınız?

listing.q: What if I do not have a job listing?
listing.a: You need one to begin, because the questions are written from it. Paste any listing for the role you are aiming at — it does not have to be a job you are applying to.

voice.a: A microphone and a browser. There is a device check before the room opens, so nothing is a surprise once the interview has started.

time.a: Six, eight or ten questions — roughly ten to twenty-five minutes. You can pause and come back; the interview keeps its place.

languages.a: English and Turkish, both fully. The interview and the report follow the language set on your account.

data.a: They are stored with the interview so the report can quote them back to you. You can delete an interview, or your whole account, at any time. The privacy notice has the detail.

closing.line: Ten minutes now, fewer surprises on the day.

privacy.title: Privacy Notice
privacy.intro: This notice explains what Interviewly collects about you, why, who else sees it, and how to get rid of it. It is written to meet KVKK (Law No. 6698) and GDPR Articles 13 and 17.

sections.heading: What we collect
sections.body: Your account: email address and, unless you sign in with Google, a hashed password. Your profile: full name, job title, date of birth, education history (school, degree, field, graduation year), hobbies and free-text interests. Your CV, if you upload one, as a PDF and as the text extracted from it. Your interviews: every question put to you, every answer you give in text or voice, and the report generated from them. Technical data: one session cookie, and server logs that record request identifiers and account identifiers, never profile field values.

sections.heading: Why we collect it, and on what basis
sections.body: To run practice interviews adapted to you and to produce a report on your answers. That is the whole purpose; we do not profile you for advertising and we sell nothing. The legal basis is your explicit consent, given at registration (KVKK Art. 5/1, GDPR Art. 6(1)(a)). You can withdraw it at any time by deleting your account, which is described below.

sections.heading: Who else processes it
sections.body: Your profile, your CV text and your interview answers are sent to large language model providers so questions and reports can be generated: OpenAI and Google (Gemini). In voice mode, your speech is additionally processed by ElevenLabs. These providers act as our processors and may process the data outside Türkiye and the EEA. Your date of birth is stripped before any profile is sent to a model. Nothing is shared with anyone else, and nothing is sold.

sections.heading: How long we keep it
sections.body: Your profile, CV and interview transcripts are kept while your account exists. When you delete your account we erase your profile, your CV file and the reports generated for you, put every transcript out of reach of the product, and overwrite your email address so it can neither sign in nor be recovered. What remains is an anonymous accounting record of what our AI usage cost, which carries nothing that identifies you.

sections.heading: Your rights
sections.body: You may ask what we hold about you, have it corrected, have it erased, and object to how it is processed (KVKK Art. 11, GDPR Arts. 15–21). Erasure needs no request: sign in and use “Delete my account”. For anything else, contact us at the address below and we will answer within thirty days.

sections.heading: Cookies
sections.body: One cookie, named “session”, which keeps you signed in and nothing else. There is no analytics cookie, no advertising cookie and no third-party tracker anywhere in the product.

sections.heading: Changes to this notice
sections.body: We record which version of this notice you accepted. If we change it in a way that affects what we collect or who we send it to, we will ask you to accept the new version rather than change it under you.

terms.title: Terms of Service
terms.intro: These terms cover your use of Interviewly. By creating an account you accept them.

sections.heading: What Interviewly is
sections.body: A practice tool. The interviews are simulations run by AI personas, and the reports are practice feedback. Interviewly is not a recruiter, does not represent any employer, and no result here has any bearing on a real hiring decision.

sections.heading: Your account
sections.body: You must be at least 18 and give accurate registration details. One account per person. You are responsible for what happens under your account, so keep your password to yourself.

sections.heading: How you may use it
sections.body: Practise as much as you like within the limits shown in the product. Do not upload another person's CV or personal data, do not paste content you have no right to use, do not attempt to extract our prompts or models, and do not automate access to the service.

sections.heading: AI-generated content
sections.body: Questions, scores and reports are generated by language models. They can be wrong, incomplete or unfair, and they are not career, legal or psychological advice. Read them as practice, not as an assessment of you.

sections.heading: Availability
sections.body: The service is provided as it is. We may change, interrupt or withdraw features, and we do not guarantee that an interview in progress will always survive an outage. Where the law allows, we are not liable for indirect loss arising from your use of the service.

sections.heading: Ending the agreement
sections.body: You may delete your account at any time from within the product, which also withdraws your consent to processing. We may suspend an account that breaches these terms, and will say why when we do.

sections.heading: Governing law
sections.body: Turkish law governs these terms, and the courts and enforcement offices of Istanbul have jurisdiction over any dispute. This does not remove any consumer protection you have where you live.

account.title: Account
account.passwordBody: Changing it is done through a reset link, so the new password is never typed into a page you are already signed in to.

preferences.title: Preferences
preferences.languageBody: Sets the interface, and the language your next interview and report are written in. A running interview keeps the language it started in.

privacy.title: Privacy and data
privacy.body: Your interviews, answers and CV are stored so the reports can quote them back to you. Deleting an interview removes it; deleting your account removes everything.

erase.title: Delete account
erase.body: Every interview, transcript, report and the CV on this account are removed. This cannot be undone and there is no way to recover them afterwards.
